question: How does the SI define a metre? Give the speed-of-light value.
raw_answer: The SI defines a metre as the length of the path travelled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second [6]. The speed of light in vacuum is defined as exactly 299,792,458 metres per second [6].

passages.heading: Metre
passages.text:
The **metre** (or **meter** in US spelling; symbol: **m**) is the base unit of length in the International System of Units (SI). Since 2019, the metre has been defined as the length of the path travelled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299792458 of a second, where the second is defined by a hyperfine transition frequency of caesium.<sup>[3]</sup>

The metre was originally defined in 1791 by the French National Assembly as one ten-millionth of the distance from the equator to the North Pole along a great circle through Paris, setting 10000 km as that quarter of the Earth's polar circumference.

passages.heading: Speed of light
passages.text: The **speed of light** is the speed of electromagnetic waves. Light travels at slower speed inside materials like glass or water; its highest speed is in a vacuum. The **speed of light in vacuum** is a universal physical constant denoted **c** (in ISO and IEC standards <sup>[4]</sup>),  exactly equal to 299792458 m⋅s<sup>−1</sup>.<sup>[2]</sup> It is exact because, by international agreement, a metre is defined as the length of the path travelled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1⁄299792458 second. The value 299,792,458 metres per second is approximately 1 billion kilometres per hour; 700 million miles per hour. For other approximations of **c**, valid for various units and size scales see the infobox. The shorter form, *speed of light*, means speed of light in vacuum in any context where the vacuum is implied.<sup>[4]</sup>

passages.heading: In unit systems
passages.text: The constant *c* is defined in the International System of Units (SI) as *exactly* 299792458 m/s. This fixed value is used to define the metre as exactly the distance that light travels in vacuum in 1⁄299792458 of a second. The second is, in turn, defined to be the length of time occupied by 9192631770 cycles of the radiation emitted by a caesium-133 atom in a transition between two specified energy states.<sup>[15]</sup> By using the fixed value of *c* and an accurate measurement of the second, the value for the standard metre is defined.<sup>[16]</sup>

sources.title: SI Unit of Length Metre and Its Modern Definition

passages.text:
Length is one of the most basic quantities measured in science. Whether we measure the distance between two cities, the size of a cell, the wavelength of light, or the dimensions of a machine, we need a reliable unit of length. The **metre (m)** is the SI unit of length and is used throughout modern science, engineering, technology, and everyday measurement.

The metre may appear to be a simple unit, but its definition has changed significantly over time. Early definitions were based on physical objects and geographical measurements. Today, the metre is defined using one of the most fundamental constants of nature: the speed of light in vacuum. This modern definition makes the unit highly precise, reproducible, and independent of any particular physical object.

passages.heading: The Metre and the Speed of Light
passages.text:
A major change occurred in **1983**, when the metre was redefined in terms of the speed of light.

The modern definition states that:

**The metre is the length of the path travelled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.**

This definition connects the metre with the speed of light in vacuum.

The speed of light in vacuum is assigned the exact value:

**c = 299,792,458 m/s**

The value is exact rather than an experimentally measured approximation within the SI system.

This means that if the speed of light and the duration of one second are known, the metre can be realized through the distance light travels during a precisely defined fraction of a second.

passages.heading: Why Is the Speed of Light Used?
passages.text:
The speed of light is an important constant in modern physics. According to Einstein’s theory of special relativity, light in vacuum travels at the same speed for all inertial observers, regardless of the motion of the source or observer.

Using this constant to define the metre provides several advantages.

First, the definition does not depend on a particular physical object. A laboratory does not need to possess an original metre bar to determine the unit.

Second, the definition can be reproduced using precise technologies such as lasers, optical frequency measurements, and advanced timing systems.

Third, the definition connects length measurement with time measurement. Since the speed of light has an exact value, extremely precise measurements of time can be used to establish extremely precise measurements of length.

Symbol: s

The second is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the cesium frequency ∆ν<sub>Cs</sub>, the unperturbed ground-state hyperfine transition frequency of the cesium-133 atom, to be 9,192,631,770 when expressed in the unit Hz, which is equal to s<sup>−1</sup>.

Symbol: m

The meter is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the speed of light in vacuum c to be 299,792,458 when expressed in the unit m s<sup>−1</sup>, where the second is defined in terms of ∆ν<sub>Cs</sub>.

Symbol: kg

The kilogram is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the Planck constant h to be 6.62607015 ×10<sup>−34</sup> when expressed in the unit J s, which is equal to kg m<sup>2</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>, where the meter and the second are defined in terms of c and ∆ν<sub>Cs</sub>.

Symbol: A

The ampere is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the elementary charge *e* to be 1.602176634 × 10<sup>−19</sup> when expressed in the unit C, which is equal to A s, where the second is defined in terms of ∆ν<sub>Cs</sub>.

Symbol: K

The kelvin is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the Boltzmann constant k to be 1.380 649 ×10<sup>−23</sup> when expressed in the unit J K<sup>−1</sup>, which is equal to kg m<sup>2</sup> s<sup>−2</sup> K<sup>−1</sup>, where the kilogram, meter and second are defined in terms of h, c and ∆ν<sub>Cs</sub>.

Symbol: mol

One mole contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10<sup>23</sup> elementary entities. This number is the fixed numerical value of the Avogadro constant, N<sub>A</sub>, when expressed in the unit mol<sup>−1</sup> and is called the Avogadro number. The amount of substance, symbol *n*, of a system is a measure of the number of specified elementary entities. An elementary entity may be an atom, a molecule, an ion, an electron, any other particle or specified group of particles.

Symbol: cd

The candela is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10<sup>12</sup> Hz, K<sub>cd</sub>, to be 683 when expressed in the unit lm W<sup>−1</sup>, which is equal to cd sr W<sup>−1</sup>, or cd sr kg<sup>−1</sup> m<sup>−2</sup> s<sup>3</sup>, where the kilogram, meter and second are defined in terms of h, c and ∆ν<sub>Cs</sub>.
